summary: SIP Back-to-Back User Agents sit on the signaling and media paths between endpoints. This standards-track RFC describes how they should behave when SRTP security is set up with DTLS.

eli5.summary: A phone-call middleman has rules for keeping a call encrypted while it is in the middle.

questions: how does dtls-srtp work through a b2bua
can a b2bua break end-to-end srtp
what is a media relay b2bua
subtitle: Rules that let SIP middleboxes sit in a call without breaking end-to-end DTLS-SRTP encryption.

tldr.problem: SIP Back-to-Back User Agents often sit between two callers and change signaling or media, which can make an end-to-end DTLS-SRTP session impossible.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists four rules: pass the certificate fingerprint and setup attribute through untouched, leave anything covered by an identity signature alone, and never change the authenticated part or authentication tag of RTP and RTCP packets.
tldr.outcome: B2BUAs that only relay or inspect media can follow the rules and keep the call encrypted end to end. B2BUAs that terminate DTLS-SRTP or modify RTP are out of scope.

sections.title: Why B2BUAs Break DTLS-SRTP
sections.content:
RFC 5763 describes how SIP can set up an SRTP security context using DTLS. The endpoints exchange a certificate fingerprint in SDP, and the fingerprint identifies the certificate that is presented in the DTLS handshake. DTLS-SRTP is defined for point-to-point media sessions with exactly two participants.

In many SIP deployments, Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs) sit on the signaling path, the media path, or both. They can modify SIP and SDP, and media-plane ones also modify RTP headers. A B2BUA that sets up a separate DTLS-SRTP session on each side makes an end-to-end session impossible. The RFC notes that B2BUAs used for address hiding or media latching can do their job without terminating DTLS-SRTP.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle of a secret conversation can ruin the secrecy if it opens the messages. This RFC says how the helper can do its job without opening them.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
The goal is guidance for B2BUAs that only terminate the media plane at the IP and transport (UDP/TCP) layers and may inspect RTP headers or RTCP packets. A B2BUA that terminates the media, or modifies RTP headers or RTCP packets, will not allow end-to-end DTLS-SRTP, and the recommendations are not expected to be applied by B2BUAs that terminate DTLS-SRTP sessions.

The RFC assumes the B2BUA is not providing identity assurance and is not authorized to terminate the DTLS-SRTP session. A B2BUA that signs identity on behalf of the endpoints behind it can change any part of SIP and SDP before signing, so nobody could tell whether it ended the DTLS-SRTP session. That case is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The rules are for helpers who only forward the mail. Helpers who want to read and rewrite the mail are not covered.

sections.title: The Four Rules for End-to-End DTLS-SRTP
sections.content:
A B2BUA MUST follow these rules to allow end-to-end DTLS-SRTP sessions:

  1. Forward the certificate fingerprint and the SDP setup attribute received from one endpoint unmodified towards the other, and vice versa.
  2. If endpoints use RFC 4474 identity assurance (the request has both Identity and Identity-Info headers), do not modify anything used to build the identity signature. That includes the entire SDP body and parts of the SIP header. Such a B2BUA cannot act as a media relay.
  3. If the newer identity mechanism (the SIP-ID draft) is used (an Identity header but no Identity-Info header), do not modify the headers used to build the signature. That mechanism does not sign material that intermediaries commonly alter, so a B2BUA can act as a media relay.
  4. Media relays and media-aware relays MUST NOT modify the authenticated portion of RTP and RTCP packets or their authentication tag.
sections.eli5: Do not change the lock, the fingerprint, or the signed parts of the message. You can change the outside of the envelope, but not what is sealed inside.

sections.title: Signaling-Plane B2BUAs
sections.content:
The RFC applies the rules to the signaling-plane categories of RFC 7092. Proxy-B2BUAs modify only the Via and Record-Route headers. None of the headers used to build the identity signature change, so they can keep working and still allow end-to-end DTLS-SRTP.

Signaling-only and SDP-modifying signaling-only B2BUAs are likely to modify headers used for the signature, for example the Contact URI. They are likely to violate rule 2 or rule 3. Depending on the application, such a B2BUA may be able to limit its changes to header fields that the identity mechanisms allow to be modified.
sections.eli5: Helpers who only stamp their name on the envelope are fine. Helpers who rewrite the signed address break the seal.

sections.title: Media-Plane B2BUAs
sections.content:
A media relay forwards every packet on a negotiated connection without inspecting or modifying the contents, changing only transport-layer and IP headers. It follows rule 1 and passes the fingerprint and setup attribute through. In the RFC's example call, Alice sends an INVITE with a=setup:actpass and a fingerprint, Bob answers with a=setup:active and his own fingerprint, and the B2BUA substitutes only its own IP address and port. The DTLS handshake then runs between Alice and Bob through the relay.

Because the DTLS handshake and the SIP answer can happen in parallel, the relay must be prepared to receive DTLS, STUN and media on the ports it advertised before it sees the answer. If RTP and RTCP are multiplexed on one port, a single DTLS connection is needed; otherwise two. With the older RFC 4474 signature a B2BUA cannot be a media relay. With the newer mechanism it can change the IP address in the c= line and the port in the m= line.

An RTP/RTCP-aware relay may inspect RTP headers and unencrypted parts of RTCP and still allow end-to-end DTLS-SRTP, since inspection reveals no clear text of the encrypted parts. One that modifies RTP headers or RTCP packets would have to act as a DTLS endpoint and re-encrypt, otherwise the integrity check fails and the endpoint drops the packet.
sections.eli5: A relay is like a mail carrier. It can read the address and swap the outer envelope, but if it scribbles on the sealed letter, the receiver will throw it away.

sections.title: Forking
sections.content:
A SIP request carrying an SDP offer can be forked to several endpoints, producing several DTLS-SRTP sessions, one between the offerer and each answerer. The B2BUA must follow rule 1 for each answer and pass each answerer's fingerprint and setup attribute through unmodified.

Each DTLS connection runs on a unique 5-tuple, so the B2BUA puts its own distinct transport address in each answer. In the RFC's example, Bob's 192.0.2.1:6666 becomes the B2BUA's 192.0.2.3:7777, and Charlie's 192.0.2.2:6666 becomes 192.0.2.3:8888. The B2BUA tracks the remote sources and ties them to the local sources used to send packets to Alice.
sections.eli5: If one call rings two phones, the helper gives each phone its own private mailbox so each secret conversation stays separate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Relays that modify RTP or RTCP, or SIP and SDP fields protected by the identity signature, are incompatible with end-to-end DTLS-SRTP and are out of scope. The security considerations of RFC 5763 also apply. The B2BUA behaviors in this RFC do not affect the security and integrity of a DTLS-SRTP session or the data sent over it.

A malicious B2BUA could try to break into the DTLS connection, but the identity validation mechanisms can prevent that. Endpoints or authentication service proxies can use them to validate peers and detect a B2BUA that terminates the DTLS connection to decrypt RTP payloads.
sections.eli5: If a helper tries to peek inside, the identity check lets the people on the call notice.
